full_judgment: 10. Every order passed by a Magistrate can not necessarily be construed as a judicial order: since a Magistrate is required to perform not merely judicial duties but administrative duties also. This dual function of a Magistrate was taken note of in the case of Abdullah Haroon and Co. vs. Cal-Cutta Corporation, reported in AIR 1950, Cal 36,where it was rightly stated that "a Magistrate has to discharge duties which are at times judicial and at other ministerial or Administrative. On certain occasions   and   under special statutory provisions, a Magistrate or a Judge may be vested with jurisdiction not as Court but as persona designata." In the aforesaid case, the question arose whether the order passed by a Municipal Magistrate under section 421 (2) of the Calcutta Municipal Act of 1923 which was a judicial order or an administrative one. Since section 531 of the said Act. empowered the Government to appoint one or more Magistrate for the trial of offences against the Act and the rules or bye-laws, thereunder, the Magistrate so appointed was found to be a Criminal Court within the meaning of section 6 of the Code and it was further found that the order which was required to be passed by such a Magistrate under section 421-(2) of that Act required exercise of judicial discretion Similarly an order passed by the District Magistrate or the District Judge may be construed as an order passed in administrative capacity or as persona designata and reference may, for such cases, be made to the decisions in the cases of Husain All Vs. Emperor, reported in A.I. R 1920, Cal 635 and Jagmohon Surujmal Vs Ven-karesh Gopal Ranade, reported in A.I R. 1933, Bom. 105. It. therefore, follows that the question whether an order is a judicial one or an administrative one is to be decided on reference to the provisions of the particular statute under which the order is purported to have been passed.
